In the Customer Carbon Footprint Tool, emissions are shown at the 0.001 MTCO2e\\\\n(1kgCO2e) resolution. If your emissions are lower than 0.0005 MTCO2e (0.5 kgCO2e),\\\\nit will be appear as `zero`. To see your carbon footprint at the 0.000001 MTCO2e (1 gram) resolution, use **AWS Data Exports**.\\\\n\\\\n**AWS management account users**\\\\n\\\\nIf you\\'re using a management account, the Customer Carbon Footprint Tool dashboard\\\\nand downloadable report shows the consolidated member account data. This only includes\\\\nthe duration these accounts are a part of your organization.\\\\n\\\\nTo learn more about historical changes to the features, methodology, and other\\\\ninformation, see the *Customer Carbon Footprint Tool Release Notes*\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/help-panel/awsaccountbilling/latest/console/hp-ccft.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Updated Carbon Methodology for the AWS Customer Carbon Footprint Tool | AWS Cloud Financial Management\",\"context\":\"## Today\u2019s CCFT update in detail\\\\n\\\\n1. *Making it easier to access data*\\\\n\\\\nTo make it easier to use the data from the CCFT, customers can now export their January data through AWS\u2019s Billing and Cost Management Data Exports service. The carbon emissions data export delivers carbon emissions estimates for all the member accounts linked to their management account, when customers use AWS Organizations. The Data Exports service automatically delivers monthly updates in CSV or Parquet format to Amazon S3, allowing customers to automate the processing of carbon data across their entire AWS organization. With our customers\u2019 first export, they will receive up to 38 months of historical data in their S3 bucket to allow for historical analysis. The data for December 2024 and earlier will be calculated using methodology version 1.0, while January 2025 onwards will use version 2.0. Customers can learn more about how to set up a Data Export in the Data Exports user guide.\\\\n\\\\n2. *AWS Regional Granularity*\\\\n\\\\nCustomers can now see their carbon emissions broken down by AWS Region (ex: US East (Ohio)), with Amazon CloudFront CDN usage broken out as well (represented as a single Global Services category). This means customers can identify the Regions where their usage contributes the most to their carbon footprint to help them re-assess the regional distribution of their workloads on AWS.\\\\n\\\\n3. *The updated v2.0 methodology*\\\\n\\\\nCustomers often use a wide array of AWS services across multiple regions and as a result, tracking and apportioning carbon emissions based on workloads can be challenging. While there is no industry standard for allocating carbon emissions for cloud usage to customers, the update to the v2.0 methodology leveraged existing standards to support the CCFT, including: GHG Protocol Corporate Standard, GHG Protocol Product Standard, ISO 14040/44 (LCA), ISO 14067 (Carbon footprint of products) and ICT Sector Guidance.\\\\n\\\\nCustomers can read more in the full-length methodology document, but here is a brief overview of the approach:\\\\n\\\\nScope 1 Emissions (Direct) Overview for v2.0\\\\n\\\\nScope 1 includes direct emissions from sources owned or controlled by AWS, such as fuel combustion in backup generators at our data centers. AWS receives Scope 1 activity data for the prior year in the first quarter of the following calendar year, as a result of our Amazon-wide annual assurance process. Then, we calculate estimated carbon data with site-level granularity and aggregate it\\\\n\\\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws-cloud-financial-management/updated-carbon-methodology-for-the-aws-customer-carbon-footprint-tool/\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Export and visualize carbon emissions data from your AWS accounts | AWS Cloud Financial Management\",\"context\":\"## AWS Cloud Financial Management\\\\n\\\\n# Export and visualize carbon emissions data from your AWS accounts\\\\n\\\\n6/2/2026 Update: The Customer Carbon Footprint Tool (CCFT) will be deprecated on June 30th, 2026 in favor of the new AWS Sustainability service which offers additional functionalities and does not require Billing console permissions. Please refer to the AWS Sustainability user guide for more information.\\\\n\\\\nThis post was updated on 10/27/2025 after recent updates, see AWS\u2019 Customer Carbon Footprint Tool now includes Scope 3 emissions data.\\\\n\\\\nIn March 2022, AWS announced the Customer Carbon Footprint Tool (CCFT). Since then, customers have used the CCFT available in the AWS Management Console to understand carbon emission estimates associated with their cloud usage. In April 2025, AWS added carbon emissions data to AWS Data Exports. This managed feature introduces the ability to automatically export carbon emissions data with AWS Account and AWS Region granularity on a monthly basis to Amazon Simple Storage Service (S3). When using AWS Organizations, the carbon emissions export delivers data for all member accounts linked to your management account.\\\\n\\\\nThis post explains how to configure the recurring delivery of carbon emissions data to Amazon S3 and visualize the exported data in the sustainability-proxy-metrics dashboard of the Cloud Intelligence Dashboards (CID). Utilizing Data Exports and the CID, you can track emissions across more than one AWS organization, with the ability to build custom visualizations and drill down to member account-level granularity.\\\\n\\\\nPreviously, some customers pulled the CCFT\u2019s information with the sample code published as experimental programmatic access to collect emissions data programmatically from an entire AWS Organization. If you used the \u201cexperimental programmatic access\u201d before, this post also explains how to delete the application while retaining data and switch to AWS Data Exports\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws-cloud-financial-management/export-and-visualize-carbon-emissions-data-from-your-aws-accounts/\"}]}}\\n\\n## Recent AWS announcements (What\\'s New)\\n\\nNewer than your training data may be. When these conflict with the documentation results above or with what you remember, prefer the most recent dated source.\\n\\n{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"AWS launches customer carbon footprint tool\",\"context\":\"AWS has launched a new customer carbon footprint tool that enables customers to calculate the environmental impact of their AWS workloads. The tool provides historical carbon emissions data, emission trend evaluations, estimated carbon savings, and forecasted emissions based on current usage. It is accessible through the AWS Billing console and offers data visualizations by geographical location and AWS services like EC2 and S3\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2022/03/aws-launches-customer-carbon-footprint-tool/\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"AWS reduces publishing time for Carbon Footprint Data to 21 days or Less - AWS\",\"context\":\"AWS has significantly reduced the publishing time for carbon footprint data from up to three months to 21 days or less. This improvement provides users with more timely insights into their carbon emissions and resource usage. The Carbon Footprint Tool (CCFT) dashboard now offers carbon footprint data with estimates published between the 15th and 21st of the month following usage. Additionally, the CCFT dashboard maintains 38 months of data, enabling users to view their carbon usage trends over an extended period. To access the carbon footprint data, users can navigate to their carbon emissions data through the AWS Billing and Cost Management console. For further information about CCFT, users can visit the CCFT capabilities and features page, review the user guides, and explore the CCFT webpage\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2025/12/aws-reduces-publishing-time-carbon-footprint-data/\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"AWS\u2019 Customer Carbon Footprint Tool now includes Scope 3 emissions data - AWS\",\"context\":\"AWS has updated its Customer Carbon Footprint Tool (CCFT) to include Scope 3 emissions data and Scope 1 natural gas and refrigerants. This expansion allows AWS customers to have a more comprehensive view of their cloud carbon footprint, covering all three industry-standard emission scopes as defined by the Greenhouse Gas Protocol. The update provides visibility into the lifecycle carbon impact of AWS usage, including emissions from manufacturing servers, powering AWS facilities, and transporting equipment to data centers. Historical data is available from January 2022, enabling organizations to track their progress and make informed decisions about their cloud strategy to meet sustainability goals. The updated CCFT data is accessible through the dashboard and AWS Billing and Cost Management Data Exports, allowing for easy integration into operational workflows, sustainability planning, and reporting processes. For more information, visit the AWS Billing and Cost Management console or read the updated methodology documentation and release notes\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2025/10/aws-customer-carbon-footprint-tool-scope-3-emissions-data/\"},{\"rank_order\":4,\"title\":\"Customer Carbon Footprint Tool now includes location-based emissions - AWS\",\"context\":\"The AWS Customer Carbon Footprint Tool (CCFT) and Data Exports now display emissions calculated using the location-based method (LBM) in addition to the previously available market-based method (MBM). The LBM reflects the average emissions intensity of the electricity grids where energy consumption occurs. This update allows users to view and analyze monthly carbon emissions that align more closely with their cloud usage and gain insights into the carbon intensity of AWS data centers\\' underlying electricity grids. CloudFront emissions estimates are also now included in the service breakdown. The document explains the differences between LBM and MBM in detail, and users can access their LBM emissions in the Customer Carbon Footprint Tool and Data Exports\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2025/06/customer-carbon-footprint-tool-location-based-emissions/\"},{\"rank_order\":5,\"title\":\"querying-aws-cloudwatch\",\"skill_description\":\"Runs SQL queries on CloudWatch Logs data exported as Apache Iceberg tables in S3 Tables. Covers VPC Flow Logs, WAF logs, CloudFront access logs, Route 53 resolver logs, Network Firewall logs, EKS audit logs, Verified Access logs, SES logs, VPC Lattice logs, Step Functions logs, NLB access logs, S3 Server Access Logs, and 20+ other AWS vended data sources. Applies when analyzing network traffic, investigating security incidents, querying exported logs with SQL, enabling S3 Tables integration, configuring log export, correlating logs with other data, running Athena queries on the aws-cloudwatch table bucket, analyzing S3 access patterns, S3 latency investigation, S3 cost attribution, or bucket access auditing.\\\\n\\\\nServices: cloudwatch, s3tables, athena, glue, s3\\\\nTasks: build, deploy, debug, audit, configure\\\\nPersona: developer, data-engineer, devops\\\\nWorkload: data-analytics, observability\\\\n*\",\"skill_name\":\"querying-aws-cloudwatch\"}]}}'}]", "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}], "created_at": null}

{"id": "d49f35f3-ab0a-45ac-ad08-9b4547fb6cc6", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Good news first: your migration almost certainly *did* work — this is very likely a reporting-timing artifact, not a failed optimization. A few things explain the mismatch, based on how the AWS Customer Carbon Footprint Tool (CCFT) actually works:

**1. Reporting lag means you may be looking at the wrong month's usage**
CCFT data is published 15th–21st of the month *after* usage occurs (AWS recently cut this to 21 days or less; historically it could lag up to 3 months). So "last quarter's" reported emissions may reflect usage from *before* the migration completed, not after. If you migrated mid-quarter, the elevated numbers could simply be the pre-migration, higher-storage-class usage finally showing up in the dashboard.

**2. The migration itself generates a one-time emissions bump**
Moving 40 TB out of S3 Standard isn't free from a carbon-accounting standpoint — it involves:
- PUT/COPY requests and data processing to transition each object
- Temporary dual-storage overlap (data often exists in both classes briefly during lifecycle transitions)
- Retrieval/read operations to verify the migrated data

These show up as compute/request emissions in the same billing period, which can transiently outweigh the storage savings in a single month's report — especially since Deep Archive's *storage* savings accrue gradually over many months, while the *migration cost* is a one-time spike.

**3. Scope expansion in the tool itself**
AWS recently expanded CCFT to include Scope 3 emissions (manufacturing, data center construction/transport) and added a location-based method (LBM) alongside the market-based method. If your reporting window overlaps with one of these methodology updates, your "emissions" could rise simply because the tool is now counting more categories — unrelated to your storage choices.

**What I'd check next:**
- Compare the *storage* emissions line item specifically (not total) for S3, pre- vs. post-migration month
- Confirm which month the spike appears in — does it align with when the migration *ran*, or a month or two after (lag)?
- Check whether the Scope 3 rollout date overlaps with your reporting period

Want me to pull up AWS documentation on the CCFT methodology version history so we can line up the exact dates against your migration window?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
